cases.description: A number means its nearest double, so two decimals with the same nearest double are one number; a runner that compares decimal text sees them differ.
Two decimals whose nearest doubles are neighbors differ; a runner that compares with a tolerance sees them equal.

-0 is 0. The reader already reads -0 as 0, so the case cannot isolate the comparison: it fails only for a runner whose reader keeps -0 and whose comparison tells the two apart, as JavaScript's Object.is does.
A number never equals a string of its digits.
A boolean never equals a number; in Python, True == 1 and True == Decimal(1) hold.
Types are compared inside arrays too; in Python, [False] == [0] holds.
A precomposed e with acute accent (NFC) differs from e followed by a combining acute accent (NFD).
Objects are equal regardless of member order.
An object with an extra member differs.
A member whose value is null differs from a missing member.
Unordered lists with the same items in another order are equal.
Unordered lists are multisets; a comparison by set sees these two as equal.
Arrays of different lengths differ; a comparison that walks only the shorter one sees [1] equal [1, 2].
The same the other way round, for a comparison that walks only its first argument.
